categories: ["ปัญหาเส้นผม", "สภาพผิว"]
synonyms: ["Irritation And Itching Of The Scalp", "Itching Scalp", "Scalp Pruritus"]
conventional_description: From a conventional perspective, an itchy scalp is most often linked to seborrheic dermatitis, dandruff, psoriasis, fungal infections, or allergic reactions to hair products. The skin becomes inflamed, flaky, or greasy, and the urge to scratch can range from mild to intense. Diagnosis is usually made through a visual exam of the scalp and sometimes a skin scraping to rule out fungal or bacterial causes.
conventional_treatments: Standard treatment typically starts with medicated shampoos containing ingredients like ketoconazole, selenium sulfide, coal tar, or salicylic acid to reduce scaling and inflammation. Topical corticosteroid lotions or solutions may be prescribed for flare-ups, and antihistamines can help with severe itching. When these don't work, oral antifungals or systemic medications may be considered.
tcm_understanding:
In TCM, the scalp is the highest part of the body, and when something is out of balance, it often rises upward like steam from a pot. The sensation of itching is almost always linked to Wind - but Wind doesn't just blow in from outside. It can be stirred up internally by Heat in the Blood, by Damp-Heat steaming from the Liver, or by Blood Deficiency that leaves the skin undernourished and vulnerable.
The Liver is central to most scalp itch patterns. Its channel runs to the crown of the head, so any heat or stagnation in the Liver system tends to travel upward. When the Liver is overwhelmed with dampness and heat - from rich food, alcohol, or chronic stress - that sticky, oily itch appears. When Liver Blood is low, the scalp becomes dry and flaky, and a subtle internal Wind creates a crawling, persistent itch that moves around.
Heat in the Blood is another common driver. This can come from a diet heavy in spicy or greasy foods, or from emotional heat like anger and frustration. The Blood carries that heat to the skin, making the scalp red, inflamed, and intensely itchy - especially after a hot shower, a glass of wine, or a spicy meal.
Because the root cause is different in each case, the treatment must be tailored: cooling the Blood, draining Damp-Heat, or nourishing Blood to extinguish Wind.
classical_quote: 「白屑风者，由风邪侵入毛孔，郁久化热，血燥生风，风热相搏，故头皮瘙痒，白屑纷飞。」
classical_translation: "White scaling wind (bai xie feng) occurs when wind evil invades the pores, stagnates over time and transforms into heat. The blood becomes dry and generates wind; wind and heat contend with each other, causing scalp itching and profuse white scales."
classical_source:
Zhu Bing Yuan Hou Lun (Treatise on the Causes and Symptoms of Diseases)  ,  Volume 27, On White Scaling Wind 									·

tcm_diagnosis:
When the scalp is red, covered with visible flakes, and the itching flares after a glass of wine or a spicy meal, a practitioner thinks first of Heat in the Blood. The tongue is red with a thin yellow coat, and the pulse feels rapid and may float. This pattern is the most acute, driven by excess Heat stirring up internal Wind, and the triggers are often dietary or environmental.
If the scalp is oily, perhaps with sticky yellow crusts or weeping, Damp-Heat in the Liver Channel is the likely picture. The tongue shows a thick, greasy yellow coating, and the pulse becomes slippery and rapid. The person often complains of a bitter taste, chest fullness, or irritability, clues that Damp-Heat is steaming upward along the Liver pathway.
A chronic, dry itch with fine white flakes and little redness points toward Liver Wind from Blood Deficiency. This pattern often brings dizziness, dry eyes, and restless sleep. The tongue is pale or red with scant coating, and the pulse is thin and rapid. It develops slowly, often in older adults or after prolonged stress has quietly depleted the body’s nourishing Blood.
When itching clearly worsens with emotional stress, frustration, or anger, the practitioner considers Liver Qi Stagnation that has transformed into Heat. The tongue has a thin yellow coating, and the pulse is wiry and rapid. Accompanying chest distension, sighing, and a feeling of internal heat confirm that constrained Liver Qi is generating Heat that rises to disturb the scalp.

patterns.symptoms: ["Scalp redness with intense itching", "Dry scaling or small red papules", "Worse with heat, alcohol, or spicy food", "Feeling of body heat, worse at night", "Thirst for cool drinks"]
patterns.worse_with: Alcohol, Spicy or greasy food, Hot weather or saunas, Emotional stress, Hot showers
patterns.better_with: Cool environment, Cooling foods (cucumber, pear), Washing with lukewarm water, Rest and calm
patterns.why_this_happens: When excessive Heat lodges in the Blood, it agitates the blood and generates internal Wind. This Wind-Heat rises to the scalp, causing redness, intense itching, and dry scaling. The Heat also consumes fluids, leaving the skin dry and flaky, while the forceful movement of Blood may cause tiny red papules or bleeding when scratched.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: red body with red spots or prickles, thin yellow dry coating. Pulse: rapid (数 shuò), often wiry or slippery.
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Heat in the Blood is a condition of excess internal Heat. Spicy food, alcohol, and hot environments add more Heat, intensifying the itching and redness. Emotional stress can also generate Heat, especially when Liver Qi stagnates and transforms into Fire. Cooling foods, cool water, and rest help drain excess Heat and calm the agitated Blood, directly soothing the scalp.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Avoid spicy, greasy, and fried foods, as well as alcohol and coffee-they add Heat. Eat more cooling foods like cucumber, pear, and mung beans. Keep the scalp clean with a mild, non-irritating shampoo and avoid very hot water. Gentle scalp massage can help, but avoid aggressive scratching.

patterns.worse_with: Greasy, fried, or spicy foods, Alcohol and coffee, Hot, humid environments, Emotional stress and anger
patterns.better_with: Cool, dry weather, Bitter and cooling foods, Light, non-greasy meals, Regular gentle exercise
patterns.why_this_happens: When the Liver and Gallbladder are overwhelmed by dampness and heat - often from rich food, alcohol, or emotional stress - that stagnant heat rises along the Liver channel, which winds up to the crown of the head. This upward steaming of damp-heat makes the scalp oily, sticky, and intensely itchy, sometimes with yellowish crusting or weeping. Because the dampness is heavy and turbid, the itch tends to linger and worsen in humid weather or after greasy meals.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: red body with redder sides, yellow greasy coating thicker at the centre and root. Pulse: wiry (弦 xián), slippery (滑 huá), and rapid (数 shuò).
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Damp-heat thrives on rich, heavy, and heating substances - greasy foods, alcohol, and stress all stoke Liver fire and generate more dampness, which then rises to the scalp. Cooling, bitter foods and a dry environment help drain the dampness and clear the heat, while gentle movement keeps Qi and fluids moving so they don't stagnate into damp-heat. Emotional calm prevents Liver Qi from knotting up and transforming into fire.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Cut back on fried, greasy, and sugary foods, as well as alcohol and coffee, which feed damp-heat. Eat more cooling, bitter greens like dandelion leaves, celery, and cucumber, and favour lightly cooked meals. Keep the scalp clean and dry, and avoid heavy, occlusive hair products that trap heat and moisture.

patterns.symptoms: ["Dry, shifting scalp itch without redness or oiliness", "Dizziness or lightheadedness", "Pale complexion, brittle or ridged nails", "Insomnia, frequent waking or vivid dreams", "Worse after menstruation or blood loss"]
patterns.worse_with: Overwork and fatigue, Emotional stress, Spicy, drying foods, Hot, dry weather, Menstruation or blood loss
patterns.better_with: Adequate rest and sleep, Cool, calm environment, Nourishing foods like black sesame and dark greens, Gentle scalp massage with moisturizing oil
patterns.why_this_happens: When Liver Blood is chronically low, the scalp loses its nourishment and becomes dry, while the unanchored Blood gives rise to internal Wind. That Wind rises to the head, producing a dry, shifting itch that can feel like a crawling sensation. This is a slower, more persistent itch-not the hot, red, oily irritation of acute heat patterns-and it often worsens with fatigue or after blood loss.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: pale, thin, possibly trembling with a thin white coating. Pulse: fine (细 xì) and wiry (弦 xián).
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Liver Blood is the anchor that keeps Wind still. Overwork, stress, menstruation, and drying foods all consume Blood, releasing Wind that rushes to the scalp and causes itching. Rest, sleep, and nourishing foods rebuild Blood and calm the Wind. Coolness and gentle massage soothe the skin without stirring up the deficiency heat that often accompanies Blood loss.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Build blood with dark leafy greens, red dates, black sesame seeds, eggs, and small amounts of liver if you eat meat. Avoid spicy, fried, and drying foods that consume yin. Prioritize sleep-blood regenerates at night. Gentle daily movement like tai chi or walking moves Qi without depleting blood, and a weekly warm-oil scalp massage can soothe local dryness.

faqs.question: How long does it take for acupuncture to stop the itching?
faqs.answer: Many people notice the itch feels calmer after the very first session, but lasting change comes with a course of treatment. For acute, heat-driven itching, weekly acupuncture for 3-5 sessions often brings noticeable relief. Chronic or deficiency-based itching may need 8-12 sessions before the cycle truly breaks. Your practitioner will adjust the frequency as your scalp settles.

faqs.question: Can I use my medicated shampoo alongside Chinese herbs?
faqs.answer: Yes, in most cases you can continue using your regular medicated shampoo while taking Chinese herbs. There are no known direct interactions between topical antifungal or anti-dandruff shampoos and the herbal formulas used for scalp itch. Just let your TCM practitioner know what you're using, and avoid applying strong steroid creams right before acupuncture on the scalp.

faqs.question: What foods make scalp itching worse?
faqs.answer: Spicy, greasy, and deep-fried foods are the biggest culprits - they generate Heat and Dampness that rise to the scalp. Alcohol, especially beer and spirits, can also trigger a flare. For many people, cutting back on sugar and rich dairy products helps reduce the oily, sticky type of itching. Pay attention to your own triggers; even one heavy meal can set off a bout of scratching.

faqs.question: Can stress really cause an itchy scalp?
faqs.answer: Absolutely. In TCM, emotional stress - especially frustration and unexpressed anger - causes Liver Qi to stagnate. Over time, that stuck energy turns into Heat, which travels up the Liver channel to the head and triggers itching. This is why many people notice their scalp gets worse during tense periods. Acupuncture and herbs that soothe the Liver often bring quick relief when stress is the main driver.

faqs.question: Is there a herbal rinse I can use at home?
faqs.answer: Yes, a gentle external wash can soothe the scalp between treatments. A common approach is to boil a combination of cooling, itch-relieving herbs like Ku Shen (Sophora root) and Bai Xian Pi (Dictamnus root bark) in water, let it cool, and use it as a final rinse after shampooing. However, the right herbs depend on your pattern, so it's best to get a recommendation from your TCM practitioner rather than trying a one-size-fits-all recipe.

faqs.question: Will the itching come back after treatment?
faqs.answer: Because TCM treats the root imbalance rather than just suppressing symptoms, the goal is long-term resolution. If you complete a full course of treatment and make the suggested diet and lifestyle adjustments, the itch often stays away. Some people may need a follow-up session or a short course of herbs during a particularly stressful season, but it's usually much milder and easier to control.
